Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I thank all delegations and participants for their contributions to this dialogue. First, I would like to take the opportunity to highlight that the report draws on 50 submissions from States, United Nations entities and other stakeholders, as well as the work of United Nations human rights mechanisms and investigative bodies. Allow me to conclude with four key messages that address the questions raised. First, impunity is not inevitable. International law provides a clear basis for accountability. The persistent gap lies in implementation. States must investigate serious violations promptly, independently, and impartially. Second, Justice must be accessible in practice. A right that cannot be exercised has no impact. Survivors need safe complaint mechanisms, legal aid, protection from reprisals, psychological support and access to health care, including sexual and reproductive health services. These services must be accessible to persons with disabilities and responsive to intersecting forms of discrimination. Third, reparations cannot be postponed indefinitely. Survivors should not have to wait for the end of a conflict or for the completion of lengthy judicial proceedings before receiving support. States should establish adequately funded programs combining restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction, and guarantees of non-recurrence. Fourth, women and children must participate in the decision that concerns them. Their participation must be safe, sustained, and capable of influencing outcomes. Women-led organizations, survivor-led groups, women human rights defenders, and children representatives should be involved in the design, implementation, and monitoring of peace, accountability, transitional justice, and preparation processes. That participation requires resources. The central call to action is therefore clear. States must translate legal commitments into institution, services and adequately funded programs that survivors can actually reach. The Council can support this effort by consistently integrating gender and child rights expertise across its mandates, maintaining attention to accountability and promoting the exchange of practical approaches that deliver results. I thank you.

Thank you very much, Vice-President. Let me start by thanking you sincerely for the trust placed in me, electing me chair of this open-ended working group for the elaboration of a legally binding instrument on the promotion and protection of the human rights of older persons. I do it with gratitude, but also with a profound feeling of responsibility, because this group does not begin today. Behind us, there are more than 10 years of ideas, debates and, as often occurs in Geneva, debates on how to continue debating. Behind all of this, there has always been a very simple conviction: older persons should be able to enjoy their human rights fully, and the international system should be better prepared to protect them. Today, this conviction is stronger than ever. The adoption of resolution 58/13 opened a new stage. It was not just another resolution to add to our libraries, which are certainly already well supplied. Rather, it was a political decision that gave us a chance to move towards something tangible: strengthening the international protection of the human rights of older persons. Since then, we have made progress. From 18 to 20 February, we held our organisational meeting. We heard from numerous actors and exchanged opinions on the stages that we had ahead. Above all, we sought to maintain and step up the political impetus that made the resolution possible. Subsequently, between 13 and 17 July, we met again. We analysed where we stood, what the challenges were and what we could do collectively to consolidate the gains that have been made. Those gains have been significant, profound and extensive. Ahead, we have a decisive moment, the session from 26 to 30 October. That is why I want to invite all of you to participate actively, not just to attend, listen or watch how the process but rather be there to build it. We need ideas, we need proposals and above all we need political will. In November, moreover, we will have the opportunity to present written contributions on various aspects and elements of the future text. That is an opportunity that must be taken advantage of. Allow me to dwell on an issue that has concerned us all this year. We all know the huge difficulties that are deriving from the liquidity crisis that the UN is experiencing. We understand the budgetary restrictions and the difficulties that the office is facing. What would have helped us, and could still help us, is something less costly than a new budgetary programme. What would help us is clear information clear information on the actual impact of the crisis in the process that was established under resolution 58/13. Greater transparency would have allowed states to better understand the limitations and, perhaps more important still, to seek joint solutions. We must avoid the one thing that a financial crisis ends up converting, almost by inertia, into a crisis of political ambition. The process deserves and has ambition. This year, we have sought to expand the conversation. We have spoken with civil society organisations, national human rights institutions, academia and other stakeholders. That is no accident. The future international framework for the protection of older persons cannot be built exclusively within the meeting chambers here in Geneva. Rather, it needs to bring on board the experience of those who work day in, day out with older persons, of those who know their needs and those who protect their rights. Their participation is not decorative; rather, it is a source of legitimacy, knowledge and tangible proposals. Moreover, another encouraging sign is that support is growing. We see that clearly in this group, in our conversations with various delegations and increasingly throughout the regional groups. That matters, because it shows that this is not just a project of a single region or a single single political group or one particular set of states. Rather, it is a project for us all, and perhaps therein lies its greatest strength. We are going through a moment when multilateralism needs to ask itself a key question: what value are we generating for our states, our societies and, ultimately, our taxpayers? We must demonstrate that multilateralism can yield results. The Human Rights Council dedicates vast amounts of time and resources to issues that often reflect profound ideological divisions. I do not question the importance of those discussions, but perhaps we can set aside part of our diplomatic talent for what should be located at the heart of our goal, which is protecting people, particularly those people in situations of greatest vulnerability. Older persons are precisely one such group. We have an opportunity to demonstrate that we can work together beyond our differences and that this council can produce something that has real consequences outside the chamber and, above all, an opportunity to build something that lasts. Our goal should not just be to conclude yet another intergovernmental process. We have had lots of processes. Our goal should be to leave an institution, a framework, a protection that continues to be useful in 10, 20 or 30 years, something that enables older persons to exercise their rights with greater effectiveness, something that helps states to protect them better, and something that allows us to look back and say that, in difficult times for multilateralism, we were able to recall why multilateralism exists. That is why I want to thank you once more for the trust deposited in me. But more than thank you, I want to ask you to maintain this commitment in October, to maintain during the next stages of resolution 58/13 the full force and energy that we have invested so far and that we should maintain it later, because the project cannot just depend on a chair, a resolution or the composition of the group on a given day. It must be converted into a collective commitment. We have ahead an opportunity that perhaps will not present itself in the same way again. We have a chance to leave for everyone an international system that is a bit more humane, a bit more effective and much better prepared to protect all of us as we get older. Thank you very much, Vice-President.

As such, we considered the duty to cooperate for the right to development, the right to peace or the prohibition of the use of force, and the possible contribution of disarmament to the realization of development. Finally, we also considered the area of climate justice. Mr. President, the working group adopted recommendations by consensus. It recommended, among others, that, one, the High Commissioner take the measures necessary to provide a balanced and visible allocation of resources and pay due attention to the visibility and effective implementation and mainstreaming of the right to development by systematically identifying and undertaking tangible projects dedicated to that right. Two, the working group should continue to convene interactive dialogues with relevant experts aimed at addressing the divergent views expressed in the working group. 3. The Working Group convene interactive dialogues with relevant experts in current trends on official development assistance, financing for development and imbalances in the international financial architecture, including international financial institutions, and assess their impacts on the realization of all human rights, including the right to development. Four, the working group convene interactive dialogues on best practices in international cooperation for the promotion of the right to development in which North-South, South-South, and triangular cooperation initiatives are presented. And five, that the High Commissioner include in his next report on the right to development and analysis of existing practices and the challenges and obstacles to the realization of that right, including unilateral coercive measures, the non-repatriation of funds of illicit origin, and the impact of the debt crisis, on recommendations on how to overcome them. On behalf of the Council, I'd like to thank Mr. Akram for presenting the working group's report. We'll now proceed with the presentation of the report of the Open-ended Intergovernmental Working Group to elaborate the content of an international regulatory framework without prejudging the nature thereof relating to the activities of private military security companies. I have the honor to give the floor to former colleague here in Geneva, His Excellency Mxolisi Sisondkosi, Chair Rapporteur of the Working Group, to present the report.

Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor for me to present the progress report on the seventh session of the open-ended intergovernmental working group to elaborate the content of an international regulatory framework without prejudging the nature thereof to protect human rights and ensure accountability for violations and abuses relating to the activities of private military and security companies. In October 2025, ahead of the seventh session, as chair rapporteur, I released the fifth draft of an international regulatory framework on the regulation, monitoring of, and oversight over the activities of private military and security companies. That fifth draft was at the center of the discussion during two days of informal intersessional consultations on 1 and 2 December 2025. On the basis of the comments and textual suggestions received during these intersessional consultations, as well as previous sessions of the working group and the expert advice from the members of the group, which was established at the third session to provide legal and technical advice on specific issues, a revised fifth draft was released in March 2026. This revised draft served as the basis for discussions at the seventh session held from 27 to 30 April 2026. The overall approach to the revised fifth draft drew on past reports of the working group and a number of existing documents, such as the International Code of Conduct for Private Security Service Providers, the Montreal Document on Pertinent International Legal Obligations and Good Practices for States Related to Operations of Private Military and Security Companies During Armed Conflict, the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, and the draft of a possible convention on private military and security companies for consideration and action by the Human Rights Council. The revised fifth draft was carefully articulated to abide by the mandate of this process and to be in a format that could form the basis for either a legally binding or a non-legally binding outcome, with language options to reflect both approaches. The seventh session was opened by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, who underscored that delegations were meeting at a time when the need for an effective international framework to regulate these activities was greater than ever. During the session, delegations reaffirmed the importance of the working group's mandate and displayed a spirit of compromise on several of the more contentious provisions. They also acknowledged that outstanding issues remain while expressing a willingness to engage with one another and to narrow the differences on these issues. For instance, between those advancing for a legally binding instrument and those supporting a non-legally binding one. The progress report on the seventh session takes stock of the work undertaken and the significant progress the working group has achieved since 2017. from the elaboration of elements of a draft regulatory framework to a revised fifth draft instrument. I would like to take this opportunity to thank all state delegations and other stakeholders for their valuable contributions and comments, as well as concrete textual suggestions made during the last session on the revised fifth draft. I would also like to thank the group of legal experts who have continued to provide legal advice on specific issues at the request of the working group and the secretariat for their ongoing support. Such active engagement with the text speaks clearly to the need for this group to continue its work to elaborate the content of an international regulatory framework relating to the activities of private military and security companies. Such a framework should ensure that human rights abuses and violations are curtailed that victims have access to effective remedies, and that states can discharge their regulatory responsibilities based on a strong international regulatory instrument. In view of this, at this session of the Council, and on the basis of the way forward adopted at the seventh session, the African Group will present a resolution requesting the extension of the working group's mandate. An extension of the mandate will allow it to continue working towards elaborating the content of an international regulatory framework, which will ultimately strengthen the protection of human rights, access to remedy, and accountability for violations and abuses relating to the activities of private military and security companies. Effective regulation, monitoring, and oversight of the activities of private military and security companies is especially important given the growing reliance on such companies, both in conflict and non-conflict settings. Let me conclude by assuring you of my commitment as chair rapporteur of the working group to ensure that the work towards the much needed framework to prevent and address the abuses and violations connected to private military and security companies continues. I thank you for your attention and support.

On behalf of the Council, I want to thank Ambassador Nkosi for presenting that report. We will now proceed with the presentation of nine thematic reports submitted by the Secretary General and the High Commissioner for Human Rights and his office. pleasure to give the floor to Mr. Dimitar Tchalev, Chief of the Equality and Non-Discrimination Branch, to present the reports.

Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, Colleagues, it's my pleasure to introduce 14 reports of the Secretary General and the High Commission for Human Rights on a range of thematic issues to be considered under item 3 and item 8. The first report is the Secretary General's report on the question of death penalty. It provides an overview of developments between July 24 and June 26. It documents the adoption of new laws abolishing capital punishment, as well as legal reforms that restricted the scope of capital offenses or further limited the use of death penalty. At the same time, the report highlights persistent and worsening challenges. global executions rose sharply in 24 and 25, largely as a result of increased use of the death penalty in small number of retentionist states. The report notes instances in which states reintroduced, took concrete step to introduce, or expanded the application of capital punishment. It further documents the continued imposition of the death penalty for offenses that do not meet the threshold of the most serious crimes under international law, particularly drug-related offenses. The report notes with particular concern developments in several states where executions increased substantially or where the death penalty was expanded or applied in ways that raise serious concerns about the lack of safeguards. It further notes the growing concentration of executions in a limited number of States. Covering the period June 2025 to May 2026, the next report is the annual report of the High Commission on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. It identifies continued gaps between international standards in the implementation of Indigenous Peoples' rights. Key concerns include inequity, recognition and protection of collective lands, inconsistent application of free, prior and informed consent, and the adverse effects of development, extractive and energy transition projects on the territories, livelihoods and cultures of indigenous peoples. The report draws attention to the challenges faced by indigenous women, children and youth, as well as threats, criminalization and reprisals affecting indigenous human rights defenders. It highlights measures taken by OHCHR to address this situation. The report recommends that States, in consultation and cooperation with Indigenous Peoples, strengthen legal recognition of collective lands, ensure free, prior and informed consent, promote inclusive participation, including that of Indigenous women, protect human rights defenders, preserve traditional knowledge and safeguard Indigenous Peoples living in voluntary isolation or initial contact. The High Commission's report on the right to development outlines all CHR activities to advance the right to development. It examines three key obstacles. Unilateral coercive measures, the non-repatriation of illicit funds, and unsustainable debt. It finds that unilateral trade, economic and financial measures can impede humanitarian action and sustainable human-centered development. States should avoid measures inconsistent with international law, ensure effective humanitarian safeguards, and address overcompliance. Illicit financial flows deprive countries of vital development resources. The report calls for the development of coherent legal frameworks that address anti-corruption, commercial and tax-related illicit financial flows through a right to development lens. Unsustainable debt can divert resources from essential services and development priorities and deepen poverty and inequality. The report stresses the need for debt relief for heavily indebted and climate-vulnerable countries, debt restructuring processes consistent with human rights obligations, increased access to grant-based and concessional financing, and debt sustainability assessment that considered human rights, development, and climate considerations. The next report is the High Commission's report on terrorism and human rights. It examines how digital technologies are reshaping terrorist threats and counterterrorism responses and their impact on the right to privacy and other human rights. Terrorists and violent extremist groups exploit dark web platforms, malware, cybercrime tools, and drones to obtain personal data, coordinate activities, and facilitate attacks. At the same time, states increasingly rely on data-driven and technologically enabled counterterrorism measures, such as fingerprinting, facial recognition, artificial intelligence, and machine learning systems. While these tools can strengthen security responses, the report finds that accountability frameworks and oversight mechanisms have not kept pace. Personal data may therefore be collected, processed, shared or retained in ways that unlawfully interfere with the right to privacy. These practices may lead to persistent surveillance and discriminatory profiling, disproportionately affecting minorities, civil society actors and journalists. Key concerns include automated content moderation systems relying on overly broad definitions of terrorists or extremists. the growing interoperability of public and private databases across institution and borders, and the growing role of private companies in counterterrorism technologies. Cross-border intelligence and data sharing arrangements also create significant privacy risks. The report recommends that states ensure that any interference with privacy is lawful, necessary and proportionate. It calls on states to refrain from using mass or indiscriminate surveillance, strengthen independent oversight and accountability mechanisms, conduct human rights impact assessment for high-risk technologies, and regulate private sector involvement. It calls on the United Nations to integrate human rights due diligence in technical assistance and strengthen independent oversight of counterterrorism measures. The next report focuses on the best practices of states local governments and other stakeholders in overcoming challenges in promoting and protecting human rights. Drawing on diverse contribution, it documents promising approaches in five areas: inclusive and participatory decision-making, public financial management, public procurement, digital governance and coordination across different levels of government. Integrating human rights into planning, budgeting, service delivery and other governance processes can strengthen inclusion and transparency while enabling public authorities to respond more effectively to inequalities and the needs of communities. The report also highlights barriers to sustaining and scaling up these initiatives. The report calls for a shift towards approaches that are institutionalized, sustainable and scalable. It encourages stronger cooperation between national and local authorities, greater involvement of local and regional governments in national human rights planning, reporting and follow-up, and continued investment in capacity building, local data, peer learning and enabling legal and fiscal frameworks. The sixth report is OHCHR's follow-up report on good practices and challenges faced by States when using the guidelines on the effective implementation of the right to participate in public affairs, with a particular focus on participation in elections. It examines good practices and challenges regarding the right to participate in public affairs, with a focus on elections, It highlights legislative and administrative measures supporting electoral and non-electoral participation, including measures aimed in increasing the participation for women and marginalized groups and initiatives promoting participation and access to information, education and awareness and participation in international forum. The report also outlines challenges including barriers to an enabling environment for the right to participation related to media freedom, peaceful process and genuine elections, crisis situation and discrimination and exclusion. OICR has jointly with Privacy International and the Carter Center developed the human rights standards and guidelines on the use of digital technologies in electoral processes. These have been released as a conference room paper. The next report is a study on the impact of mental health challenges on the enjoyment of human rights by young people. Drawing on a wide range of submissions and consultations with many young people from all regions, it highlights the significant mental health challenges and human rights challenges experienced by youth. Young people identified anxiety, depression, burnout, loneliness, trauma, self-harm, and suicidal ideation as key concerns. These are shaped in part by structural and social determinants, including poverty, inequality, discrimination, violence, conflict, displacement, inadequate standards of living, digital harms, and multiple planetary crises, as well as a lack of social connection. These challenges disproportionately affect youth facing multiple or intersecting forms of discrimination. The study identifies significant structural and systemic barriers related to the availability, accessibility, acceptability, and quality of mental health services, including chronic underinvestment, lack of expertise, limited youth-friendly and community-based services. These barriers undermine the enjoyment of a wide range of young people rights, including the right to health, education, decent work and social security. The study calls for a youth-centered, human rights-based approach developed together with young people. It recommends integrated government action, community-based and rights-compliant services, meaningful youth participation, sustainable financing, disaggregated data and stronger accountability. The next report is the High Commission's report on civil society space. It sends a clear message. Safeguarding civic space is not only about preventing restrictions, but ensuring that all people can participate safely and meaningfully in decision making that affects their lives. Protecting and promoting civic space is not optional, but an investment in resilient societies, more effective institutions, and more inclusive, a safer future for all. Based on the inputs received from a wide range of stakeholders, the report identifies several major global trends. First, digital technologies have created new opportunities for participation mobilization, yet this goes hand in hand with increased surveillance, censorship, online attacks, and disinformation. Artificial intelligence is amplifying these risks. Second, Social movements, often led by young people, continue to mobilize around inequality, corruption, economic hardship, environmental concerns and exclusion. However, many of those movements face excessive force during peaceful processes, peaceful protests, criminalization and stigmatization. Third, Restriction on civic space are becoming more sophisticated. Governments increasingly rely on counter-terrorism, cyber crime, public security, foreign influence laws, as well as burdensome administrative requirements on associations to constrain legitimate civic activity. Funding restrictions are major. and major reductions are further weakening civil society organization. The report recommends five priority actions: strengthen solidarity and partnerships, improve monitoring and exposure of emerging restriction, expand protection mechanisms for those at risk, invest in sustainable and flexible funding, and promote positive inclusive narratives. The next report focuses on the human rights challenges in addressing and countering all aspects of the world drug problem. Drawing on 100 contributions, it finds that drug policies affect women and girls in distinct ways that reinforce existing discrimination. The female prison population is growing faster than the male population, although many women commit drug-related offenses amid violence, poverty, or coercion. Sentencing often overlooks these circumstances and caregiving responsibilities. Fear of punishment, prosecution during pregnancy, or loss of child custody deters women from seeking treatment and health care. Only one in 18 women with drug use disorders receives treatment, compared with one in seven men, and services often neglect women's specific needs. The report recommends reducing punitive responses, expanding alternatives to incarceration, considering decriminalization and responsible regulation, ensuring voluntary gender-responsive health and harm reduction services and alternative development, involving women meaningfully in drug policy-making, and aligning prevention measures with human rights. The Secretary-General reports on genocide prevention. focuses on early warning and timely action, reviewing national, regional and international developments. It calls for adequately resourced national prevention mechanisms with clear mandates, regular risk assessment using the framework of analysis for atrocity crimes, and the translation of their findings in practical national strategies. States should also strengthen or establish such mechanisms and to appropriately integrate genocide prevention into bodies with related mandates, including national human rights institutions. The report outlines United Nations support for genocide prevention, including through the Office of the Special Advisor on the Prevention of Genocide, and encourages the Human Rights Council to strengthen access to data on genocide risk indicators, including hate speech and discrimination against groups protected by the Genocide Convention. Next, I introduce the OHCHR study on protection gaps of vulnerable segments of the population regarding access to medicine and vaccines in the context of the right of everyone to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. The report shows complex, interconnected barriers still preventing many people, especially vulnerable and marginalized communities, from accessing medicines, vaccines, and essential medical products. It also notes the need for better regulation, of the private sector and the return to a multilateral trading system that enables the full use of existing TRIPS flexibilities and puts an end to disruptive tariffs, sanctions and other trade measures that unduly restrict or interrupt medical supply and change. The report then analyses how other trends such as increased attacks on health care, environmental degradation, including climate change, the digital transformation of health systems, and regressive narratives are undermining science-based health policy, impede access to medicine, vaccines, and other medical products. The report reaffirms the need for a holistic human rights-based approach underpinned by international cooperation and solidarity that tackles the underlying barriers preventing access to medicines, vaccines, and other medical products. Human rights defenders rely on digital technologies to connect, document abuses, speak out, and protect themselves. Yet, the rapid expansion of state and corporate power online has not been matched by adequate safeguards, accountability or oversight. Drawing on three regional workshops and consultations with human rights defenders, civil society and the private sector, This report on due diligence and improved responses to the risk of digital technology to human rights defenders, indeed identifies three principal concerns. First, restrictive regulation. Vague cybercrime offenses and overboard national security, counterterrorism, and online harms laws can be used to criminalize defenders. censor their work and enable surveillance. Second, pervasive surveillance. Defenders are targeted with intrusive spyware, while advances in AI are making both target and mass surveillance cheaper and more scalable. Third, online censorship and attacks. Internet shutdowns, arbitrary content restrictions, Smear campaigns, manipulated content and cyber attacks increasingly undermine defenders' work and safety. The report also finds that corporate responses remain insufficient and seem to be declining. The report calls on states to align laws and regulations with international human rights standards strengthen safeguards against transnational repression, protect personal data, and regulate surveillance technologies. Companies should respect human rights, increase transparency, and resist abusive state requests. Greater support is also needed for civil society efforts to prevent and respond to digital threats. I now turn to the final two Secretary General reports on OHCHR technical cooperation on national human rights institutions and on the NHRIs compliance with the Paris Principles. These reports fall under item 8. The first report on national human rights institutions summarizes OHCHR and wider United Nations support to establish and strengthen national human rights institutions. The report draws on inputs received from 19 member states, 23 national institutions and UNDP under the tripartite partnership program of OHCHR, UNDP and GANRI. OHCHR together with other United Nations entities, provided technical assistance to over 50 national institutions across regions, advising on enabling legislation and compliance with the Paris Principles, building institutional and staff capacity, strengthening thematic human rights practice, and facilitating engagement with the international human rights system. The report encourages States to establish and strengthen independent NHRIs' compliance with the Paris Principles and use of OHCHR technical support in this regard. It also encourages States to provide NHRIs with a broad human rights mandate by granting them adequate powers of investigation, including the competence to visit places of deprivation of liberty. The report further encourages States to take the measures necessary to protect the staff of NHRIs, human rights defenders and other individuals that cooperate or seek to cooperate with them. The second report concerns the activities of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions in accrediting national institutions in compliance with the Paris Principles. The UN UNCHRD peer review mechanism assesses NHRI compliance with the Paris Principles and measures Sustainable Development Goal indicator 16.8.1. During the reporting period, the subcommittee considered 51 NHRIs. As of June 26, 119 human rights institutions are accredited by the subcommittee, of which 91 are fully compliant with the Paris Principle, A status, and 28 are partially compliant, B status. The reviews conducted during the reporting period revealed systemic compliance issues. Across all regions, the subcommittee identified shortcomings in the procedures for selecting and appointing leadership of national human rights institutions, in the breadth of the mandate of these institutions, including with respect to conduct by private actors and to unannounced visits to places of deprivation. in the adequacy and timeliness of their funding and in the consistency of their engagement with international human rights system, including through human rights mechanisms. For the sake of promoting the dignity and well-being of all.

Venezuela reaffirms that all human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and their full implementation requires social and economic conditions enabling all people to live with dignity and participate equitably in the benefits of development. To that end, the right to development is an essential component. Finally, Venezuela urges all States to step up genuine international cooperation based on dialogue, solidarity, mutual respect and sovereign equality of states and rejects all forms of selectivity and political instrumentalisation of human rights. Only through multilateral action, grounded in the UN Charter and aimed towards overcoming structural inequalities, will it be possible to move towards a more just, equitable and inclusive international order for the benefit of all peoples. Thank you.

Thank you.

Mr. Vice President, the full enjoyment of human rights depend not only on legal guarantees, but also on the conditions that enable people to live in safety and dignity, access essential services, and sustain their livelihoods. Ensuring this condition is also integral to sustainable development and to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda. This linkage becomes particularly evident in post-conflict situations where recovery and development are essential to restoring the conditions necessary for the full enjoyment of human rights. Following the restoration of its sovereignty and territorial integrity, Azerbaijan has undertaken extensive reconstruction and rehabilitation efforts to restore affected areas and facilitate the safe and dignified return of former IDPs. Landmines, however, continue to impede this process. Beyond threatening life and physical security, they hinder the reconstruction of infrastructure and restrict people's ability to return to work and rebuild their lives. Therefore, the impact of landmines extends across the civil, political, economic, social, and cultural dimensions of human rights. Recognizing this reality, Azerbaijan has designated mine action as its national SDG 18, reflecting the essential role of demining in sustainable development. A sustainable post-conflict recovery can't be achieved while such barriers remain. Advancing mine action is therefore an investment not only in safer and more resilient societies, but also in the effective realization of human rights and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. I thank you.

Vice President. Those glaring steps by the German authorities make it clear that they will restrict the rights of West German citizens to take part in cultural life. From today, they will not be able to visit concerts, exhibitions or use the Pushkin library or take Russian language courses. Mr. Vice President, The death penalty abolition marks a historic step in Lebanon. This commitment has been forged through successive crises but also sustained by important rays of hope. Yet, in recent years, the Lebanese population has continued to endure Israeli hostilities, particularly in the south, resulting in loss of life, occupation, mass displacement, destruction of homes, civilian infrastructure, and agricultural lands, environmental damage, disruption of essential services, including health care and education, as well as enforced disappearances and detention. into forced confessions, and their families are warned and intimidated.
